title: "Your AI assistant and Python environment"

## Before the first meeting

If you have time before our first meeting on **28 October 2026**, look through this guide and try starting the setup. Begin with an assistant, then prepare the Python environment. Jan with Blablador is our suggested example; you can also use an assistant you already have, such as Claude or Codex. On Windows, setting up Ubuntu through WSL 2 beforehand is particularly helpful because it can require a restart or administrator access.

Bring your laptop and charger if you can. We will show the tools in use and reserve **about 30 minutes to set them up together**. An unfinished installation is fine. Keep any error message and the command that produced it, and bring them along. If your setup already works, use that time to explore the first notebook and check a calculation with a partner.

## The course setup

I will demonstrate **Jan connected to Blablador first**, so that we have an assistant available while installing Python and working through errors. We will then use **uv to manage Python and packages** and **marimo to work in notebooks**. You can follow the same exercises with another assistant. If Jan is difficult to install, Blablador also has a web interface. If service access is unavailable, work with a partner or ask the instructor for help and continue with the Python setup.

These tools have different jobs. Python executes the calculations. uv keeps the course's dependencies together. marimo is the interface for writing and running Python. Jan is a chat interface. Blablador runs the language model on remote infrastructure.

The [glossary](glossary.qmd#computing-and-the-course-tools) provides short definitions of the computing terms below. We will also explain them as they become useful.

Start with the [assistant](#set-up-the-ai-assistant) and try a short debugging conversation. If you already have one, you can go straight to the [debugging example](#assistant-for-debugging). Windows users then prepare [Ubuntu in WSL 2](#windows-wsl). We will use its Linux shell for the course. Continue with the [computing basics](#computing-basics) and [Python setup](#set-up-python). Once the notebook runs, we will check an assisted calculation. A separate code editor is optional.

## Set up the AI assistant {#set-up-the-ai-assistant}

### Why Jan and Blablador? {#why-this-assistant}

Jan is one example of how we can work with open models. You are welcome to use **Claude, Codex, or another assistant** for the course. You do not need to buy a subscription or replace a tool that already works for you. In each case, we will practise explaining the problem, examining the proposed answer, and checking what it does.

We suggest Jan with Blablador because it gives us access to [open models](glossary.qmd#open-models) through research infrastructure in Germany. [Jan is open-source software](https://www.jan.ai/); Blablador supplies the models, running at Forschungszentrum Jülich. The service is free to use, subject to access and usage limits. This gives us an option that does not depend on each student maintaining a paid subscription. [Helmholtz's service introduction](https://www.hifis.net/tips/2025/05/05/tip-llm/); [Jülich's account of the open-model service](https://strube1.pages.jsc.fz-juelich.de/2026-06-12-hdc-rs/); [current access and limits](https://sdlaml.pages.jsc.fz-juelich.de/ai/guides/blablador_api_access/)

### Where does the conversation go? {#assistant-data}

With this connection, Jan sends the conversation to Blablador at Jülich. The model runs there, even though Jan is installed on your laptop. Choosing an open model, choosing where it runs, and choosing how a service handles your data are separate decisions.

Blablador's emphasis on protecting conversation content makes it worth considering for research where confidentiality matters. Before using unpublished or confidential material, check that the particular service and configuration are approved for that data by your institution or project. Hosting in Germany is a useful consideration, but does not by itself settle that question. We use public or synthetic data for the course exercises.

The details depend on how you connect. For example, the operator's March 2026 description says the main web interface does not retain chats or uploaded files, but records IP addresses for operation; the separate staging interface saves conversations and files. Those web-interface statements should not be treated as a description of every client or API configuration. Also consider any history saved by your chosen client. [Blablador's description of its web interfaces](https://lists.fz-juelich.de/hyperkitty/list/blablador-news@lists.fz-juelich.de/thread/LMBPE2FH7I7O6HZA5DX2SIQLI7A2WUIX/)

### Install Jan

If you would like to use this setup, install [Jan Desktop](https://jan.ai/download) and open it. We will connect it to a model running at Jülich; this step can be completed before setting up Python.

On Windows, select the installer matching x64 or ARM64. For older Macs, check current support: Jan's documentation describes limitations on Intel Macs. If the app is unsuitable, use the [Blablador web interface](https://blablador.fz-juelich.de/) for the same teaching task. [Jan Windows installation](https://docs.jan.ai/desktop/install/windows); [Jan Mac installation](https://docs.jan.ai/desktop/install/mac)

### Blablador access

Follow [Jülich's current access guide](https://sdlaml.pages.jsc.fz-juelich.de/ai/guides/blablador_api_access/). It describes university/EduGAIN sign-in to Helmholtz Codebase and a personal [access token](glossary.qmd#api-key), a credential for accessing the service, with the `read_user` scope. Use your own token. If your institutional login is not accepted, contact the instructor; the exercise also includes an example you can check without an account.

Keep the token out of notebooks, chat messages, screenshots, and submissions. Enter it only in the intended provider's credential field. A local chat application connected to Blablador sends the prompts to that service; “local app” does not mean local inference.

### Connect Jan to Blablador

Jülich publishes a [specific guide for using Blablador with Jan](https://sdlaml.pages.jsc.fz-juelich.de/ai/guides/blablador_jan_ai/). In the app:

1. Open **Settings → Model Providers → Add Provider**.
2. Choose the **OpenAI-compatible** [API](glossary.qmd#api) format if the dialog asks for one, and name the provider **Blablador**.
3. Enter the connection settings below, then save.
4. Refresh the model list if necessary, open a chat, and select a Blablador model.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Base URL | `https://api.blablador.fz-juelich.de/v1` |
| API key | Your own Blablador token |
| Initial model | `alias-code` for code assistance; `alias-fast` is another starting option |

The API-format name describes compatibility; it does not require an OpenAI account. Jan's current [custom-provider documentation](https://docs.jan.ai/desktop/remote-models/custom-endpoint) describes the same connection mechanism. Menu wording can change with Jan releases.

Use the remote provider directly. This exercise does not require downloading a local language model, starting Jan's local API server, configuring tool access, or installing GPU drivers.

Blablador's [model aliases](glossary.qmd#model-alias) can change which underlying model they serve. Record the date, alias, and actual model identifier when available for an assessed comparison. [Blablador API guide](https://sdlaml.pages.jsc.fz-juelich.de/ai/guides/blablador_api_access/)

### Try a debugging conversation {#assistant-for-debugging}

Before moving on to Python, send a message using your chosen assistant. If you have just connected Jan to Blablador, select one of its models. We can start with a problem that needs no working Python environment:

> I am about to set up a Python course project. Suppose a setup command reports that it cannot find the project's pyproject.toml file. Help me work out what to check before reinstalling anything. Ask which operating system I use, explain one check in plain language, and tell me what its result would help us distinguish.

The project file may be absent, or we may be looking in the wrong folder. Checking the current folder and its contents helps distinguish those possibilities. In the next section, we will learn the commands for doing that. A reply confirms that the connection works; the proposed explanation is something we still need to check.

Keep the chat available during Python setup. When an actual error appears, give the assistant enough context to investigate it:

```text
I am following the course setup using uv and marimo.
Operating system and environment (for example, Windows with Ubuntu in WSL 2):
Where I entered the command (for example, Ubuntu's Bash shell or a notebook cell):
Command or code:
Error message:
What I expected:
What I have already tried:

Explain the error in plain language. Ask for missing information.
Suggest one check at a time and explain what its result would tell us.
Use the supplied course project and its locked dependencies.
```

Remove tokens and private details from the error text before sharing it. Read the suggested check, predict what it might show, then run it and compare the result. Use the course instructions and official documentation as references if the advice differs. Keep the original error and the change that resolved it; they will help you recognise the problem next time.

If the assistant connection is still blocked, continue with the computing basics and ask the instructor or a partner for help. Python setup does not depend on having a chat account.

## Windows: Ubuntu in WSL 2 {#windows-wsl}

**Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)** lets us run a Linux environment on a Windows computer. We will use **Ubuntu in WSL 2** for uv, Python, and the notebooks. Jan stays a Windows application, and the Windows browser will display marimo. macOS and Linux users can continue to the computing basics.

### Prepare Ubuntu once

If Ubuntu in WSL 2 is already available, open it from the Start menu. Otherwise, follow [Microsoft's WSL installation guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), with instructor or IT support if needed. On a supported Windows system, the installation command is:

```text
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

This is a **one-time Windows installation step**: run it in Windows Command Prompt opened with **Run as administrator**, then restart if requested. It prepares the Linux environment where the course work will happen. Arrange help in advance if your laptop is managed or you cannot install system components. [Microsoft's environment setup guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/setup/environment)

Open **Ubuntu** from the Start menu and create its Linux username and password when prompted. Password characters will not appear while you type. This Linux account has its own home folder. In Ubuntu, check the distribution's WSL version with:

```bash
wsl.exe --list --verbose
```

The Ubuntu row should show **VERSION 2**. If it does not, ask the instructor to help with the existing installation. From this point, enter course commands in **Ubuntu's Bash shell**. You can also select the Ubuntu profile in Windows Terminal. [WSL commands and version check](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/basic-commands)

If WSL installation is blocked, use pair work or the instructor's supported notebook service while arranging help. You can still follow the examples and use Jan.

## Before typing commands {#computing-basics}

“Open a terminal and create an environment” is a short instruction with quite a few assumptions hidden inside it. We will unpack those before using the tools. You can return to this section when a setup step becomes unclear.

### Terminal, shell, and command

A **terminal** is the application window in which you type commands and see their output. A **shell** is the program inside it that interprets those commands and launches other programs. On Windows, our Ubuntu terminal runs Bash inside WSL. macOS Terminal commonly runs zsh; Linux terminals often run Bash. The window and the program doing the interpreting have different jobs.

Open **Ubuntu** on Windows, or **Terminal** on macOS or Linux. The text beside the cursor is the **prompt**: the shell is ready for a command. Examples elsewhere may begin with `$` or `%` to represent a prompt. Leave those markers out when copying a command. Our command blocks omit them. [Missing Semester: introduction to the shell](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/course-shell/)

### Folders, paths, and “where am I?”

A **directory** is a folder. Every shell session has a **working directory**, the folder from which it interprets relative file locations. Opening a folder in your file browser does not automatically move an already open shell there.

Try these two commands, one line at a time, pressing Enter after each:

```bash
pwd
ls
```

`pwd` displays your working directory; `ls` lists its contents. These commands work in the Bash and zsh shells we use, including Ubuntu inside WSL.

A **path** is an address for a file or folder. An absolute path starts from the filesystem root, such as `/Users/yourname/Downloads` on macOS or `/home/yourname` in Ubuntu. A relative path starts from the working directory. For example, `notebooks/00-getting-started.py` means “look inside the `notebooks` folder here.” The shorthand `~` refers to your home folder in the current environment.

`cd` changes the working directory. After extracting the setup kit below, if `ls` shows the folder `digital-chemistry-intro`, enter it with:

```bash
cd "digital-chemistry-intro"
```

If it is elsewhere, use `cd` followed by its path in this environment, enclosed in quotes. Quotes keep a path containing spaces together. Run `pwd` and `ls` again: you should now see `pyproject.toml`. `cd ..` moves to the parent folder, and `cd ~` returns to your home folder. Changing directory changes where the shell looks; it does not move your files.

In WSL, keep the course project under your Linux home folder, for example `/home/yourname/digital-chemistry-intro`. A Windows Downloads folder and an Ubuntu home folder are different locations. The [project download step](#get-the-supplied-project) shows how to move the kit between them. [Microsoft: working across file systems](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/filesystems)

### Python, packages, and a virtual environment

**Python** is a programming language. A **Python interpreter** is the program that executes Python code. A **package** supplies reusable code: NumPy, for example, provides tools for numerical arrays. A package that our project needs is a **dependency**.

Different projects can need different versions of the same package. A **virtual environment** gives a project its own Python interpreter configuration and installed packages. Ours lives in a folder called `.venv` on your computer. Keeping those packages separate lets us update one project's software without changing another project's environment. [Python tutorial: virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3.12/tutorial/venv.html#introduction)

**uv** manages this environment for us. Three names in the project have distinct roles:

| Name | Role in this course |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | Describes the project, its Python requirement, and the packages it needs. |
| `uv.lock` | Records the resolved package versions and their dependencies. |
| `.venv` | Contains the environment installed on your machine; uv creates it during setup. |

You may encounter instructions to **activate** an environment. Activation changes which programs your current shell finds by default. We use `uv run` to select the project's environment for each command, so the setup below needs no separate activation step. [uv: working on projects](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/projects/)

### Notebook, cell, and dependencies

A **notebook** brings explanations, code, and results together. We use **marimo**, which saves the text and code in a Python (`.py`) file and displays the notebook in your browser. A **cell** is one block of the document. Code cells calculate; Markdown cells contain formatted explanations.

Suppose one cell defines a concentration and another uses it to predict an absorbance. The second cell **depends on** the first. When you edit and run the concentration cell, marimo's automatic mode reruns the prediction cell too. This is called **reactivity**. The order follows the dependencies in the code, which need not be the order of cells on the page. [How marimo runs cells](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/reactivity/)

A notebook-wide variable name must be defined in one cell. To change `concentration`, edit its existing definition rather than assigning it again elsewhere. Reactivity does not check whether a formula is scientifically appropriate. It also does not track every change made inside an existing object; for now, keep a calculation and its intermediate changes together in one cell.

| What you want to do | Where it belongs |
|---|---|
| Run `uv sync --locked` to prepare the environment | The shell in your terminal |
| Run `print(2 + 2)` as Python | A notebook code cell, executed with Shift+Enter |
| Write an explanation or a heading | A notebook Markdown cell |

In our setup, marimo's server and the Python calculations run on your computer. The browser displays their interface. On Windows, they run inside Ubuntu in WSL; the browser remains a Windows application. The `.py` file stores the instructions. The running Python process holds variables and produces outputs. Closing a browser tab is not the same as stopping the server. The setup below shows how to reopen the saved file in a fresh process.

[The Missing Semester of Your CS Education](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/) explains many of the tools that programming courses tend to take for granted. Its [introduction to the shell](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/course-shell/) develops the commands we have just used. Windows users can try its Unix-shell examples in Ubuntu through WSL. I recommend it if you would like to understand more of what happens around your Python code.

## Set up Python

### 1. Install uv

Use the [official uv installation instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/). Python does not need to be installed separately: uv can obtain the version requested by the course. [Python management with uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/install-python/)

On **Windows**, open Ubuntu in WSL. Use the **Linux** installer there; Linux users can use the same command:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

This downloads and runs uv's official installer. Open a new terminal in the same environment after it finishes so the shell finds the installed command. If `curl` is unavailable, the official installation page also provides a `wget` alternative. Install uv in the environment where the Python code will run.

On **macOS**, if Homebrew is already installed:

```bash
brew install uv
```

Otherwise, use the standalone installer above, which also supports macOS. Installing Homebrew solely for this class is unnecessary.

Confirm that the new terminal recognises the command:

```bash
uv --version
```

### 2. Get the supplied project {#get-the-supplied-project}

Download and extract the [introductory setup kit](downloads/introductory-setup.zip). The `digital-chemistry-intro` folder contains `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, the notebooks, and a short check script.

**Windows with WSL:** extract the ZIP using Windows File Explorer. Then, in Ubuntu, open your Linux home folder in File Explorer:

```bash
cd ~
explorer.exe .
```

Copy the extracted `digital-chemistry-intro` folder into that window. Back in Ubuntu, enter the copied project:

```bash
cd ~/digital-chemistry-intro
ls
```

You should see `pyproject.toml`. Keep the project and the `.venv` we will create inside this Linux folder. [Opening WSL folders in File Explorer](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/filesystems#view-your-current-directory-in-windows-file-explorer)

**macOS or Linux:** open a terminal and [navigate](#folders-paths-and-where-am-i) to the extracted `digital-chemistry-intro` folder.

If you already have the full teaching project, use its `course` directory instead. You should see `pyproject.toml` in the folder from which you run the following commands.

### 3. Create and check the environment

Run these commands in **Ubuntu on WSL**, or in your macOS/Linux terminal:

```bash
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked python scripts/check_environment.py
uv run --locked marimo edit notebooks/00-getting-started.py --headless
```

The first command installs the supplied package versions into `.venv`. The second checks imports, a small fit, and plot rendering. The third opens the getting-started notebook in marimo without trying to launch a browser. Keep its terminal running while working. No environment-activation command is required. [Using uv with marimo](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/marimo/)

Copy the complete local URL printed by marimo into your browser, including its access token. It begins with `http://localhost:...` or `http://127.0.0.1:...`. On Windows, use your Windows browser to reach the server running in WSL. Use the port printed in your terminal; do not assume a particular port. Keep this token-bearing URL out of the debugging chat. [marimo command reference](https://docs.marimo.io/cli/); [WSL: accessing Linux applications from Windows](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/networking#accessing-linux-networking-apps-from-windows-localhost)

Read the second command as “use uv to run this project's Python interpreter on the file `scripts/check_environment.py`.” Here `run` is uv's subcommand, `--locked` is an option, and the final argument is a relative file path. `--locked` makes uv report an error if the supplied lockfile needs updating, rather than changing the package selection during setup. [uv: locking and syncing](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/sync/)

The supplied project sets marimo to run on opening and to rerun dependent cells automatically. If you change this setting, the execution controls are in the notebook footer. [marimo runtime settings](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/configuration/runtime_configuration/)

The introductory environment uses Python 3.12 and contains marimo, NumPy, and Matplotlib for our first two notebooks. We will add packages as the chemistry and deep-learning exercises need them.

### 4. Change a calculation

The launch command opens `notebooks/00-getting-started.py`. Run the notebook if marimo prompts you to do so. In **1. A prediction**, calculate the expected absorbance before reading the output. Change `concentration` from `0.5` to `1.0` and run the edited cell with Shift+Enter. The prediction cell should update too: 0.55 becomes approximately 0.95. Now change `slope` and follow which other results change.

To check which interpreter a notebook is using, add a code cell:

```python
import sys
print(sys.executable)
print(sys.platform)
```

The interpreter path should refer to this project's `.venv`. In WSL, expect a Linux path ending in `.venv/bin/python` and `sys.platform` equal to `linux`. Launching marimo with `uv run --locked` from the supplied project selects that environment; no separate kernel selection is needed.

To keep the supplied starter, make a copy of its `.py` file in the same `notebooks` folder with your file manager and open that copy in marimo. Save your edits. Then stop the server with Ctrl+C in its terminal and reopen your copy with the same launch command, replacing the filename. This checks that the saved instructions can recreate the calculation. You are ready when you can change an input, explain the result, and reopen a working copy.

For lecture 2, stop the first server with Ctrl+C and open the calibration notebook:

```bash
uv run --locked marimo edit notebooks/02-calibration-lab.py --headless
```

The kit also contains HTML previews in `notebooks/previews/` with code and recorded results. These are for reading: their controls do not rerun Python. They load marimo display assets from the internet; the separate calibration browser activity is the offline fallback. Open the `.py` notebook in marimo to change a calculation.

### Check your bearings

Before moving on, answer these in your own words:

1. Why could `uv sync --locked` work in the terminal but give a syntax error in a Python cell?
2. A notebook cannot import a package that was installed for another project. What would you inspect first?
3. One cell defines a concentration; another predicts absorbance from it. What should happen when you edit and run the first cell?

<details>
<summary>Compare your explanation</summary>

1. It is a shell command that launches uv. An ordinary Python cell expects Python code.
2. Check the notebook's `sys.executable` and the folder from which you launched marimo. The package may belong to another project's environment.
3. In automatic mode, marimo reruns the dependent prediction cell. If automatic execution is disabled, it marks dependent cells as needing to run. Either way, the notebook file and installed packages are separate from the running calculation.

</details>

## Check an assisted calculation {#first-task-with-the-assistant}

Once marimo is working, use the calibration example, where a check is easy to calculate independently:

> I am learning Python. I have predictions [2, 0] and observations [1, 1]. Help me calculate the mean squared error. Ask me to try the calculation first, then help me test a Python implementation. Keep the example small and explain the inputs and outputs.

Calculate the two residuals and their squared errors yourself. Run the suggested implementation in marimo. Try an exact prediction as a second check. Write down one suggestion you accepted or corrected and the evidence for that decision.

A fluent answer is a proposal to inspect. Keep the units, data selection, and scientific interpretation in view when the tasks become more complex.

## An assistant that works on files {#cli-assistant}

Once this setup works, we will also try a [coding assistant in the terminal](cli-assistant.qmd). It can read a Python file, change it, and run a calculation. We will use the small error calculation from lecture 2 to examine each of those steps and check the result ourselves. Codex CLI with Blablador is our starting example; an assistant you already use is welcome too. We will make time for this together in a later practical, so it is not another installation to complete before the first meeting.

## When something does not work

| Symptom | First useful check |
|---|---|
| Ubuntu is unavailable, or WSL setup needs administrator access or a restart | Ask the instructor or IT for installation support; use pair work or the supported notebook service meanwhile. |
| `uv` is not recognised | Open a new terminal; confirm installation using the official instructions. |
| On Windows, uv or Python resolves to a Windows installation | Open Ubuntu and use the Linux uv installation and project folder. Check the notebook's interpreter and `sys.platform`. |
| The project cannot be found | Open a terminal in the extracted folder containing `pyproject.toml`. |
| The WSL notebook does not open in the browser | Keep its Ubuntu terminal running and copy the printed localhost URL into the Windows browser. If it fails, ask for support with WSL networking. |
| A package imports in the terminal but not in the notebook | Inspect `sys.executable`; stop the server and launch marimo with `uv run --locked` from the course project. |
| Package installation is blocked or too slow | Ask for the available browser environment or pair with a neighbour; record the error for follow-up. |
| A variable is defined in two cells | Edit its original definition, or give the new quantity a different name. |
| A changed value does not update a result | Run the edited cell; check whether automatic execution is disabled or a cell has an error. |
| Jan cannot list models | Check the provider URL, token, and token scope privately; follow the current service guide. |
| A model request is rate-limited | Wait as instructed by the service or use the prepared example; repeated retries do not fix capacity. |
| Jan will not run on the laptop | Use Blablador's browser interface. |
